tldr: The authors propose MINT, a unified foundation model that reconstructs world-space hand motion directly from egocentric RGB video. In a single forward pass, it jointly predicts camera trajectories, 3D bimanual poses, and hand observability. Powered by a 1,021-hour pseudo-labeled dataset and two-stage training, MINT operates in real time (44.1 fps) and achieves high-accuracy zero-shot generalization without external detectors or SLAM.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of MINT. Given a 32-frame video window, a pretrained Geometric Context Transformer (GCT) extracts spatiotemporal features. Four dedicated heads then jointly predict camera extrinsics, field of view (FoV), bimanual MANO parameters, and hand observability.
overview:
Recovering camera and hand 3D trajectories in world coordinates from egocentric video is critical for robot imitation learning and augmented reality. However, existing approaches rely on multistage pipelines strung together in series: hand detection, monocular depth estimation, SLAM camera tracking, hand mesh recovery, and trajectory refinement. This setup allows detection misses and occlusions early in the pipeline to propagate downstream, all while incurring massive computational costs.

To address this, the authors introduce MINT, a unified foundation model. It shares a spatiotemporal geometric representation of the video and resolves camera and bimanual motion in a single forward pass. By linking camera and hand geometry through differentiable coordinate transformations, the model learns mutual geometric constraints simultaneously. To tackle the lack of ground-truth data needed to train such a large model, the authors built EgoPipeline, an automated system that generates accurate pseudo-labels from public video datasets (Ego4D, EPIC-KITCHENS, and EgoDex), creating a 1,021-hour structured dataset.

Experiments evaluated MINT zero-shot on unseen benchmarks (HOT3D and ARCTIC). MINT matched or outperformed multistage teacher pipelines in camera pose and hand reconstruction accuracy. It achieved an inference speed of 44.1 fps (22.7 ms per frame) on a 4-GPU setup, demonstrating a significant speedup over the original pipeline and enabling real-time processing.
contributions: Proposed MINT, a unified model that jointly estimates camera trajectories, field of view, bimanual MANO poses, and hand observability flags in a single forward pass from a shared spatiotemporal geometric representation.
Constructed EgoPipeline, an open-source pipeline that automatically generates high-quality world-space hand and camera trajectory pseudo-labels from large-scale egocentric videos.

Established an effective two-stage curriculum training strategy that first learns geometric relationships on large-scale pseudo-labels and then corrects metric scale errors using a small set of high-quality data.
Released a curated 1,021-hour egocentric structured 3D motion trajectory dataset, along with training and inference code.

sections.heading: Where Prior Methods Fall Short and How MINT Differs
sections.summary: The paper reviews prior work across three domains: egocentric video understanding, monocular hand pose estimation, and feedforward 3D reconstruction. It highlights how conventional multistage pipelines suffer from error propagation and high compute overhead, positioning MINT as a direct spatiotemporal geometric model for hand motion.
sections.details:
### II-A Egocentric Video Understanding and Robot Learning
Large-scale egocentric datasets like Ego4D and EPIC-KITCHENS are widely used for human activity understanding and robot learning (such as ViTRA and EgoMimic). However, extracting 3D hand trajectories from these videos for robot manipulation requires combining calibration, depth estimation, SLAM, and hand reconstruction, demanding enormous compute and engineering effort.

### II-B Video-Based Hand Pose Estimation
Methods predicting MANO parameters (joint angles and shapes) from monocular images (like HaMeR and WiLoR) and video-based methods (such as HaWoR and ViDiHand) have advanced considerably. Still, they remain confined to camera-frame hand recovery or depend on multistage setups with external SLAM trajectories, failing to capture end-to-end geometric relationships between the camera and hands.

### II-C Feedforward 3D Reconstruction
Recently, feedforward methods like DUSt3R and LingBot-Map have emerged, predicting camera poses and scene geometry via transformer forward passes without iterative optimization. MINT builds on LingBot-Map's clip-level geometric context transformer (GCT), extending the paradigm beyond static scene geometry to dynamic, articulated bimanual motion reconstruction.

sections.heading: How EgoPipeline Automatically Generates 1,021 Hours of Training Data
sections.summary: The authors developed a pipeline to automatically extract high-quality world-space hand and camera trajectories from daily real-world videos. Integrating multiple models with rigorous post-processing and filtering yielded 1,021 hours of structured motion supervision.
sections.details:
Real-world egocentric videos offer diverse scenes and actions, but lack 3D ground truth for hands and cameras. To bridge this gap, the authors collected 1,729 hours of video from Ego4D, EPIC-KITCHENS, and EgoDex, and built EgoPipeline, an automated annotation pipeline.

The process works as follows:
- **Detection and Filtering**: YOLO detects hands in the video. Clips where hands are absent for more than one second, or broken clips showing three or more hands, are discarded.
- **Parallel Camera and Hand Reconstruction**: For surviving clips, GeoCalib estimates camera intrinsics and rectifies distortion. Next, MoGe-2 monocular depth maps are fed into MegaSaM (or DROID-SLAM) to recover scaled camera trajectories. Concurrently, HaWoR estimates camera-frame bimanual MANO parameters and 6-DoF wrist poses.
- **Post-processing and World Transformation**: To mitigate spikes and dropouts from hand detection failures, the pipeline applies median absolute deviation (MAD) outlier rejection, spherical linear interpolation (SLERP) for missing frames, and unscented Kalman filter (UKF) smoothing. Finally, it composites these with camera trajectories to produce world-space bimanual motion.

Through this process, the authors built a highly reliable, large-scale dataset of 1,021 hours of supervision.

sections.heading: Inside MINT: A Unified Model with Shared Geometric Representations
sections.summary: MINT extracts spatiotemporal geometric features from a video window and predicts camera pose, field of view, bimanual MANO parameters, and hand observability using four dedicated heads. Differentiable coordinate transformations link camera and hands, while two-stage curriculum learning achieves accurate metric scale recovery.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Visual Geometric Backbone and Long-Form Inference
The model takes a 32-frame window (resolution $378\times 518$) as input and tokenizes image patches with DINOv2 ViT-L/14. These tokens are concatenated with camera tokens, register tokens, and scale tokens, then fed into the Geometric Context Transformer (GCT). The GCT alternates between intra-frame attention and global temporal attention to integrate geometric context across frames. For long videos, a sliding-window strategy chains trajectories in $SE(3)$ and fuses overlapping frames, keeping memory complexity linear with respect to video length.

### IV-C Prediction Heads and Geometric Coupling
Four task heads directly regress motion from the extracted features:
- **Structured Hand Pose Head**: Using four learnable queries for wrist translation, wrist rotation, 15 joint rotations, and hand shape, it outputs temporally consistent MANO parameters (218 dimensions total for both hands) across two residual iterations.
- **Camera Head**: Iteratively estimates camera translation $\bm{t}_t$ and rotation quaternion $\bm{q}_t$ through a causal trunk while conditioning on past predictions. Field of view (FoV) is regressed via an independent lightweight branch to prevent interference.
- **Hand Observability Head**: Predicts the probability that hands are validly observed in each frame, filtering out noise from occlusions and out-of-frame movements.
- **Differentiable Hand-Camera Coupling**: Camera-frame wrist positions $\bm{p}^c_{t,s}$ and rotations $\bm{Q}^c_{t,s}$ are transformed directly into world coordinates using predicted camera poses. Because this transformation is differentiable, world-space errors backpropagate simultaneously to both camera and hand heads.

### IV-D Two-Stage Training Strategy
- **Stage 1 (Joint Geometry Learning)**: The backbone and all heads are trained jointly using large-scale pseudo-labels from EgoPipeline. Camera loss, MANO loss, hand presence loss, and world-space consistency loss are optimized together, instilling relative hand-camera geometric relationships.
- **Stage 2 (Camera Scale Calibration)**: Monocular SLAM pseudo-labels suffer from global scale ambiguity. In this stage, the geometric encoder and hand heads are frozen, and only the camera head is fine-tuned on accurate camera trajectories from real teleoperation setups to correct metric scale and pose errors.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Zero-Shot Accuracy Meets Real-Time Inference
sections.summary: Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D and ARCTIC benchmarks showed that MINT matches or outperforms multistage baselines. Stage 2 training drastically reduced scale error, and the single forward-pass architecture enabled high-speed inference at 44.1 fps.
sections.details:
### V-A & V-B Hand Pose Estimation and Temporal Smoothness
On HOT3D, MINT reached a hand detection accuracy (FAcc) of 0.940. This significantly outperformed zero-shot WiLoR (0.827) and approached in-domain trained ViDiHand (0.948). The joint position error (PA-MPJPE-p) reached an impressive 10.70 mm.
In terms of temporal smoothness, MINT's forward-pass predictions exhibited less jitter than optimization-based baselines, and applying UKF smoothing at inference further reduced jitter by 79%.

### V-C Camera Trajectory and the Impact of Stage 2
For camera trajectory evaluation, MINT achieved a relative translation error (RPE-T) of 3.39 mm on ARCTIC, outperforming MegaSaM (8.73 mm). While its absolute trajectory error (ATE) does not match global-optimization SLAMs like DROID-SLAM due to the lack of loop closure, Stage 2 training showed dramatic benefits. On HOT3D, the arc length ratio (scale factor) improved from 0.466 after Stage 1 to 1.094—close to the ground truth of 1.0—slashing ATE from 524.7 mm down to 181.7 mm.

### V-D Ablation Studies
Comparing training data mixtures revealed that combining EgoDex and EPIC-KITCHENS with Ego4D (MPJPE-p: 23.61 mm) yielded better zero-shot generalization than training on Ego4D alone (25.32 mm). Replacing the pretrained GCT backbone with random initialization significantly worsened joint error and jitter (degrading from 11.52 to 18.44), proving the value of geometric pretraining.

### V-E Inference Throughput
On a single GPU, MINT runs at 72.4 ms per frame, achieving a 1.45x throughput improvement over HaWoR (105.1 ms/frame). With distributed parallel processing across 4 GPUs, window processing parallelizes cleanly to reach 22.7 ms/frame (44.1 fps), surpassing video playback rates for true real-time execution.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Directions
sections.summary: MINT recovers world-space camera and bimanual motion end-to-end from egocentric video. Combining large-scale automated labeling with a unified architecture establishes a promising new standard for accurate, fast motion understanding.
sections.details:
This work introduced MINT, eliminating the need to chain multiple standalone models by solving world-space camera and bimanual trajectories in a single transformer forward pass. Leveraging 1,021 hours of automated supervision and two-stage training, it demonstrated outstanding zero-shot generalization across unseen domains at a fast 44.1 fps.

At the same time, residual scale drift from the monocular reconstruction pipeline is not entirely resolved, and chaining 32-frame windows leaves open the risk of long-term trajectory drift. The authors plan to incorporate more accurate metric scale supervision to achieve stable, long-horizon trajectory recovery in future work.

takeaways: Demonstrated that traditional multistage pipelines (hand detection -> SLAM -> mesh recovery) can be unified into a single forward-pass spatiotemporal geometric transformer.
Proved the effectiveness of connecting camera and wrist poses via differentiable coordinate transformations, allowing the model to learn relative geometric constraints end-to-end.
Established a practical two-stage curriculum strategy: learning relative geometry on large monocular SLAM pseudo-labels, then fine-tuning metric scale on a small set of high-quality data.
Showed that window-based processing yields high parallel throughput during inference, making real-time execution (>44 fps) feasible for robot learning applications.
limitations: Because training data relies on monocular SLAM pseudo-labels, the model cannot completely escape inherent scale drift.
Chaining fixed 32-frame windows without a global loop closure mechanism makes the system susceptible to accumulating global position drift over very long videos.
Camera-frame wrist translation error (depth direction) remains notably larger compared to the accuracy of joint angle reconstruction.
